stimulus.text:
Henry Ford, with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922), Chapter X, “How Cheaply Can Things Be Made?” (verbatim excerpt):

"The payment of high wages fortunately contributes to the low costs because the men become steadily more efficient on account of being relieved of outside worries. The payment of five dollars a day for an eight-hour day was one of the finest cost-cutting moves we ever made, and the six-dollar day wage is cheaper than the five."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt from Henry Ford, My Life and Work (Garden City, New York: Doubleday, Page, 1922), Project Gutenberg eBook #7213, public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Henry Ford, My Life and Work (1922), Project Gutenberg eBook #7213
stem: Ford's claim that the six-dollar day is “cheaper than the five” best illustrates which idea?

options.text: Wages should fall whenever prices fall
options.misconception: Ford never says wages should fall with prices. He says high wages cut costs, which let prices fall.

options.text: Higher pay can lower cost per car
Workers themselves should own the factories
options.misconception: Ford says nothing about workers owning the factories. He kept ownership and paid high wages instead.

options.text: Cheap cars always need cheap labor
options.misconception: Ford's point is the opposite: cheap cars came from well-paid labor. Cheap labor was not his method.

rationales.A: Ford never says wages should fall with prices. He says high wages cut costs, which let prices fall.
rationales.B: Ford says the six-dollar day is “cheaper than the five” because better-paid men work more efficiently. Paying more lowered the cost of each car.
rationales.C: Ford says nothing about workers owning the factories. He kept ownership and paid high wages instead.
rationales.D: Ford's point is the opposite: cheap cars came from well-paid labor. Cheap labor was not his method.
rationales.general:
1. Read the claim literally: six dollars a day costs Ford less than five.
2. Ask how that can be true: the better-paid man builds more cars per hour.
3. State the idea: the cost that matters is the cost per car, not the wage per day.
4. Apply it: a higher daily wage still wins when each car takes fewer paid hours to build.
Remember: compare costs per unit made, not costs per worker paid.
